atoms.a: Jackson can play the guitar. He wants to learn to play his favourite song in one week by practising every day.

feedback.wrong: This is a SMART goal. Jackson wants to learn a specific song that is important to him. He can easily measure whether he is able to play the song and, as he can already play the guitar, it is achievable. He also gave himself a clear timeframe to reach the goal.

atoms.a: Emily’s dance teacher wants her to learn a new step that is for students three levels above Emily.

instruction.text: Which SMART criteria does the goal not have?

feedback.finish: Emily does not want to reach the goal herself, and it is most likely beyond her abilities to achieve it. There is also no clear deadline by when the goal should be completed.

atoms.a: Amanda gets £10 pocket money every week. She wants to save £100 in four weeks to buy a new toy.
atoms.sound: Amanda gets 10 pounds pocket money every week. She wants to save £100 in four weeks to buy a new toy.

instruction.text: Which SMART criteria does the goal not have?

feedback.finish: With the pocket money Amanda gets, she cannot save £100 in four weeks. The goal is not achievable.

atoms.a: Drew wants to memorise the multiplication tables up to 12 before his maths test by practising for 15 minutes each day.

feedback.wrong: This is a SMART goal. There is a specific number of multiplication tables and it is easy to measure whether Drew knows them. The task is achievable, and Drew set the goal for himself. He also has given himself a deadline.

atoms.a: Ashton wants to help his parents a little this week.

instruction.text: Which SMART criteria does the goal not have?

feedback.finish: Ashton could be more specific about exactly how he wants to help and how often. This would also make it easier for him to determine if he has reached his goal.
